topic: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Examinations
text:
Examinations have long been used to measure knowledge, compare performance, and award qualifications. The rise of generative AI has challenged many assessment practices, especially unsupervised take-home tasks. Educational institutions must now reconsider what examinations should measure and how genuine student ability can be demonstrated.

Traditional examinations remain useful because they can test what students can do without external assistance. Supervised written papers may become more important in subjects where independent recall and reasoning are essential. However, closed-book examinations do not always reflect how people work in professional environments.

An alternative is to permit limited AI use during assessment. Students may be asked to use AI tools and then evaluate the output, identify errors, or improve the response. This approach tests both subject knowledge and AI literacy. It may better reflect workplaces where technology is available but human judgement remains necessary.

Oral examinations can also provide stronger evidence of understanding. Students may explain their reasoning, answer follow-up questions, and defend decisions. Practical demonstrations, presentations, and project-based assessments may further reduce dependence on written outputs alone.

Nevertheless, new examination formats can create challenges. Oral and practical assessments require more staff time and may be difficult to apply to large groups. Institutions must also ensure that students receive equal access to approved tools and accommodations.

Assessment policies should state clearly when AI is allowed, restricted, or prohibited. Inconsistent rules may confuse students and produce unfair disciplinary outcomes.

AI will not eliminate examinations, but it will change their design. Future assessment should combine supervised knowledge checks, practical work, oral explanation, and responsible AI use. The goal should be to evaluate understanding, judgement, and application rather than the ability to produce a polished answer.
